title: Quantifying Thickness and Puncture Resistance of Solitary Bee Cocoons
author: Wasserman, Wootton, et al.
materials: Timing: 2–4 h for printing and assembly

steps.title: Measure Cocoon Dimensions
steps.instruction: Select 10–15 cocoons (≈3–5 min per cocoon). Measure length along the longitudinal axis to the nearest 0.1 mm. At three locations (middle, nipple end, base end) take two perpendicular width measurements each, recording to the nearest 0.1 mm. Enter cocoon ID, sex (if known), length, and all width measurements into a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. Using the collected size range, design a cutting stencil; for Osmia lignaria a 7 × 2 mm stencil yields on average 5–7 segments per female cocoon and 3–4 per male cocoon.

substeps.instruction: Select 10–15 cocoons from the sample population.
Measure longitudinal length to 0.1 mm.
At middle, nipple end, and base end, record two perpendicular width measurements each to 0.1 mm.
Log ID, sex, length, and all width values in Excel.
Design a 7 × 2 mm stencil based on the measured ranges.

steps.title: Print and Clean 3D Fixtures
steps.instruction: Print the custom 3D‑printed parts required for cutting, mounting, and puncture testing (clamps, tower mount, 7 × 2 mm cutting stencil, bottom fixture 6 × 5.5 mm, top fixture with Luer‑Lock). Use the printing parameters described in the Materials and Equipment section (≈2–4 h total). Remove burrs and overhangs with a single‑edge razor blade, then clean all components with 70 % ethanol before use. Adjust designs as needed for compatibility with the MTS Synergie 100 clamps and needle type.

substeps.instruction: Print clamps for holding cocoon segments onto the tower mount.
Print the tower mount used for thickness measurement with the CellScale MicroTester.
Print the cutting stencil having a 7 mm × 2 mm opening.
Print the bottom fixture with a 6 mm × 5.5 mm opening.
Print the top fixture for needle mounting with an integrated Luer‑Lock adapter.
Remove any burrs/overhangs with a razor blade.
Clean all printed parts with 70 % ethanol.

steps.title: Prepare C‑cards from Plastic
steps.instruction: Rinse clear craft plastic sheets, trim to 31 × 31 cm, and cut C‑cards using a Silhouette Cameo 4. Set the Type B AutoBlade to 10 and a 3 mm Kraft Blade to 15–20. Perform 2–4 passes with the AutoBlade followed by 6 passes with the Kraft Blade using the custom design in Silhouette Studio 4.5. The resulting C‑cards have a 4.75 mm central gap for mounting cocoon segments.

substeps.instruction: Rinse the outer layer of the clear plastic sheet with warm water.
Trim the sheet to 31 × 31 cm to fit the cutting mat.
Load the sheet into the Silhouette Cameo 4.
Select Type B AutoBlade (set to 10) and run 2–4 passes.
Select 3 mm Kraft Blade (set to 15–20) and run 6 passes.
Cut the custom C‑card design (Figure 1) producing a 4.75 mm gap.

steps.title: Prepare Glass Cutting Mat
steps.instruction: Wash two semi‑tempered glass panes with soap and water. In a well‑ventilated area, spray an even coat of black paint on one side of each pane (or on a single pane), applying additional coats until no bare spots remain. Allow the paint to dry fully, then align the panes so the painted sides face inward and secure all edges with laboratory‑label tape.

substeps.instruction: Wash both glass panes to remove dust.
Apply an even coat of black spray paint to one side of each pane.
Repeat painting until the surface is uniformly covered.
Let the paint dry completely.
Align the panes with the painted sides facing each other.
Tape the edges of the stacked panes with laboratory label tape.

steps.title: Extract Bee, Determine Sex, Cut Segments
steps.instruction: For each cocoon (≈2.5–3.5 h for 10 cocoons, yielding 30–50 segments): place the cocoon on a black glass mat, cut off the nipple with a razor blade, make a longitudinal cut with dissecting scissors, and extract the adult bee with forceps. Inspect both bee and cocoon for parasitoid, bacterial, or fungal infection; discard if infection is present. Determine sex by morphology (males: metallic blue‑green, white facial hair patch, longer antennae; females: larger, stout, larger mandibles, no extensive white facial hair, shorter antennae, horn‑like prongs, scopa). Record sex and condition. Place the two cocoon halves on the black glass surface, cut each half into quarters longitudinally using a ruler and scissors. Align the 7 × 2 mm 3D‑printed stencil parallel to the cocoon’s longitudinal axis and cut the defined segment with an X‑ACTO knife. Transfer each segment to a pre‑labeled gelatin capsule, avoiding damage or stretching.

substeps.instruction: Place cocoon on a black glass mat for contrast.
Cut off the nipple (cap) with a razor blade and discard it.
Make a longitudinal opening with dissecting scissors.
Extract the adult bee using dissecting forceps.
Inspect bee and cocoon for signs of infection; discard if infected.
Determine sex using morphological traits and record in the data sheet.
Place the two cocoon halves onto the black glass surface.
Cut each half into quarters longitudinally with a ruler and scissors.
Align the 7 × 2 mm stencil parallel to the cocoon’s axis.
Cut the segment along stencil edges with an X‑ACTO knife.
Transfer the excised segment to a pre‑labeled gelatin capsule.

steps.title: Verify Puncture Sites and Analyze Data
steps.instruction: After puncture testing (1–3 days for verification), tape the mounted C‑card back onto a microscope slide with transparent tape and examine under a light microscope. Confirm complete needle penetration (no incomplete holes or lateral tearing) and capture digital images with Motic software. Discard data from specimens with incomplete penetration. Export raw load (N)‑displacement (mm) data from MTS TestWorks as .txt files, import into a pre‑formatted Excel sheet using a comma delimiter, and create columns for zeroed displacement, zeroed load, maximum load, maximum displacement, stiffness, work to puncture, normalized load, and normalized work. Zero displacement: Dactual = Datpoint – Dstarting; zero load: Factual = Fatpoint – Fstarting. Identify the start point where load begins to rise, apply zeroing formulas until a sharp drop to near zero. Compute: max load (Fpeak = max Factual), max displacement (Dpeak = max Dactual), stiffness (ΔF/ΔD from the initial linear region using ~20 points), work to puncture (integral of F(D) from 0 to Dpuncture via trapezoidal rule), normalized load (tmean / Fpeak), normalized work (tmean / Wpuncture) where tmean is the mean segment thickness per sex. Copy load and displacement columns to a new tab, plot displacement (mm) vs. load (N), apply a 5‑point moving average if noisy, and generate load‑displacement curves. Create a summary table for each test group containing all measured properties, calculate mean and standard deviation with Excel’s AVERAGE and STDEV functions, and compile a final summary table with test‑group ID, means, and SDs. Verify all calculations with representative samples before processing the full dataset.

Inspect the puncture site under a light microscope at multiple magnifications.
Confirm a clean puncture hole with no incomplete penetration or tearing.

Discard data from specimens with incomplete penetration.
Export raw load‑displacement data from MTS TestWorks as .txt files.
Import the .txt files into the pre‑formatted Excel template (comma delimiter).

steps.title: Perform Statistical Analysis
steps.instruction: Using Microsoft Excel and OriginPro 2025, present data as mean ± SD and set significance level α = 0.05. For thickness, average 20 measurement points per segment (n = 6 cocoons per sex) and assess normality with the Shapiro‑Wilk test; test variance homogeneity with Levene’s test. If normal, conduct one‑way ANOVA between sexes. For mechanical testing data (n = 10 segments per group, total 40 specimens), assess normality with Shapiro‑Wilk; if non‑normal (p < 0.05), use Kruskal‑Wallis across the four groups (Female‑Up, Female‑Down, Male‑Up, Male‑Down). When Kruskal‑Wallis is significant (p < 0.05), perform Dunn’s post‑hoc pairwise comparisons. Raw data are available from the corresponding author on request.

substeps.instruction: Present all results as mean ± standard deviation.
Set statistical significance threshold at α = 0.05.
For thickness measurements (20 points per segment, n = 6 cocoons/sex), run Shapiro‑Wilk normality test.
Run Levene’s test for variance homogeneity.

If normality is violated (p < 0.05), apply Kruskal‑Wallis test across the four groups.
When Kruskal‑Wallis shows significance (p < 0.05), conduct Dunn’s post‑hoc pairwise comparisons.
Document that raw data are available from the corresponding author upon request.

description:
Solitary bees, comprising approximately 75% of all bee species, are essential pollinators in agricultural and natural ecosystems.1,2
Osmia lignaria Say (Hymenoptera: Megachilidae) is a solitary bee, commonly known as the blue orchard mason bee, and is an important orchard pollinator in the western United States of America (USA).3,4,5 Some solitary bees, such as O. lignaria, construct a silk-based cocoon during development.6,7,8 The cocoon serves as a protective barrier during development, separating the prepupa from environmental stressors and parasitoid threats.5,9,10 Parasitic wasps, including Monodontomerus spp., target the pupa or prepupal stage by penetrating the cocoon with their ovipositors to inject eggs or paralyze the host.5,11,12 Parasitoid wasps use alternating ovipositor valve movements to reduce buckling risk during substrate penetration,13 with recent biomechanical analyses estimating maximum first valvula protraction forces of approximately 1.19 mN based on muscle cross-sectional areas and estimated muscle tension in Diachasmimorpha longicaudata.14 Despite the functional importance of solitary bee cocoons, many aspects remain understudied, such as the cocoon puncture resistance properties, especially compared to the extensively studied silkworm cocoons.15,16,17,18,19
